#3176. This Magnetic Phone Neck Mount Was the Easy Filming Solution I Needed, and It's on Sale for Black Friday

I write a lot about e-readers and e-ink tablets for Lifehacker, and one issue I'm constantly grappling with is how to write informatively about a bunch of devices that can be quite different in some details, like build or native firmware, and pretty much identical in others, given that literally all e-ink devices use display technology produced by the same Chinese company. (It's called E-Ink.) The best way to do this is to include more video in my articles, but I've lacked a good way to film hands-free so I can easily demonstrate a device's look and feel—until recently.

I recently got an offer to try out a magnetic neck mount from Telesin, a low-cost option to turn my iPhone into a wearable so I can keep my hands free while filming. It's a pretty basic concept, but well-executed: The band that goes around your neck is made of rubber with a firm but flexible core, so you can easily position it to be longer or shorter or at an angle, and the phone mount is on an extending arm with three joints to give you additional options.

I haven't had a chance to film anything for public consumption quite yet, but my testing has already given me some great ideas for how I can use it to show off, say, what it's really like to use a micro-reader in comparison to a full-sized Kindle, as I'll be able to wear it to give a more accurate user's point of view. And right now is a good time to pick one of them up, as many of Telesin's phone and camera accessories (including similar models built to handle an action camera like a GoPro) are discounted for Black Friday; the one I tested is down to $17, or 15% off.

This won't be the right device for every filming scenario. Though MagSafe holds my iPhone fairly securely, I found that I would accidentally detach it every time I tried to adjust the shooting angle—once even leading me to drop it. That's potentially bad news, as using it may require you to take the phone out of its case if it isn't MagSafe-compatible. (Mine isn't.) But if you're just looking for an inexpensive way to shoot hands-free video in a controlled environment, it could be exactly what you need.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON: If extreme weather doesn’t shutter theaters in the Northeast, then Lionsgate is looking forward to a lucrative Thanksgiving stretch with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping potentially banking $85M+ over five-days.

Should the sixth title in the Suzanne Collins series file in that range, it will rep the second best Thanksgiving haul for a Hunger Games movie after Catching Fire‘s $109.9M Wednesday-Sunday turkey take 13 years ago. Sunrise on the Reaping‘s Wednesday is looking like $15.5M-$16.5M with a second 3-day weekend around $58M-$65M at 4,018 theaters, -46% to -51%. Five day forecasts are always a challenge for the industry to predict: Business dips on Thanksgiving then spikes on Black Friday, which is one of the most active moviegoing days of the year. By Sunday, we’re looking at a running cume for the Francis Lawrence directed movie of $233M domestic, which would be 40% higher than the lifetime cume on 2023’s Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

Second will either be Disney’s Hexed at 3,725 theaters or Universal/Paramount’s Focker-in-Law at 3,382 sites. Hexed is seeing around $7.8M today (including $2.1M previews), for a 3-day around $20M and 5-day between $35M-$40M. Let’s see if this picks up before passing complete judgement on this $200M original animation production, but it’s clear Hexed isn’t Coco or Frozen. Watch on Deadline

Focker-in-Law is seeing a $5.2M Wednesday, 3-day of $24.8M and 5-day of $36.1M. No Rotten Tomatoes audience scores yet on either title.

Fourth goes to Paramount’s third frame of Johnny Depp Christmas movie, Ebenezer with $1.5M today at 3,180 sites and a 3-day between $6.8M-$7.3M, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

WEDNESDAY AM: As we told you last night, Lionsgate scored its best Tuesday ever at the domestic box office with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and the best ever for the Suzanne Collins franchise as the day raked in $15.98M.

2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire owned the previous best Tuesday for the franchise with $15.96M. Running cume for the fifth Francis Lawrence movie is $148.1M and by Thanksgiving, Sunrise on the Reaping will surpass its previous 2023 chapter’s lifetime domestic B.O. of $166.3M.

As we told you, Sunrise on the Reaping will dominate the Thanksgiving Wednesday through Sunday stretch as the franchise has historically done before since 2013, this time with a floor of $70M+. Previously, the pics over Thanksgiving cooked up the following: Catching Fire ($109.9M), Mockingjay Part 1 ($82.6M), Mockingjay Part 2 ($75.9M) with Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes way behind ($42.2M).

Lionsgate has had back-to-back global hit openings this year with Sunrise on the Reaping last weekend at $226.1M WW and Michael with $218.8M. This has all happened under the administration and watch of Motion Picture Chairman, Adam Fogelson. Still no word out there whether or not Lionsgate rejected or accepted Legendary’s bid.

Walt Disney Animation’s Hexed came in with $2.1M, $100K above the $2M we were spotting yesterday. That preview figure is higher than Encanto ($1.5M previews, 5-day of $40.5M) and Wish ($1.8M previews including $500K Saturday sneaks; 5-day of $31.6M). No RT audience score yet, but critics were meh at 67% fresh. There is a chance that the traditional Disney pic comes in lower than its 5-day forecast of $40M-$45M as original animated titles are very challenging to launch in the streaming era, but you have to start some place.

Universal and Paramount’s Focker-in-Law, which didn’t have previews last night, rather began showtimes at midnight, has more potential to hit its 5-day forecast of $45M given the Ariana Grande factor and the fact that audiences love the franchise. The first Meet the Parents 26 years ago was the fave among critics at 85% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Focker-in-Law isn’t the worst at 26%, as that belongs to 2010’s Little Fockers. 2004’s Meet the Fockers stands at 39%.

Hexed, Focker-in-Law and Sunrise on the Reaping are sharing PLFs with the latter having Imax screens (except for AMC where they are being designated to Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth).

Thank God for Lionsgate Hunger Games at the box office: Sans a Wicked, Moana and a Zootopia, the Thanksgiving box office will certainly be down from last year’s five day robust $290.3M, which was the fifth best ever. Moana 2 and Wicked led the holiday to its best haul ever with $424.9M.

#3169. Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” …

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting company to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

#3166. TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026 list includes a shot taken on iPhone 18 Pro

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition)

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

#3165. Mayor Zohran Mamdani Says Famed Balloons Will Soar Again At Rescheduled Macy’s Parade: “It’s The Only Inflation We Support In New York City”

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani struck a personal note during a press briefing Wednesday about the postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade due to a major storm.

“Many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow,” the mayor said. “I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first. On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker, and everyone visiting, will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe.”

Organizers and city officials, made the call earlier Wednesday to push the 100th annual edition of the parade to Saturday morning, when the forecast calls for sunny skies and temperatures in the 40s. A Nor’easter, a classic storm pattern, is expected to bring drenching rain and high winds to New York and many other parts of the Northeast on Thursday and into Friday. Forecasters are calling for as much as 2 inches of rain in New York, which would make it among the wettest Thanksgivings ever in the city.

Officials have rules in place preventing balloons from proceeding down city streets when sustained winds are 25 mph or higher, or if gusts top 35 mph. Watch on Deadline

Mamdani, hobbled by a recent Achilles tear, said he will miss Saturday’s parade due to pending surgery and “doctor’s orders.” But while he walked with a limp, the mayor showed he hadn’t lost a step mentally. When a reporter asked about the blowing up of the signature balloons, an annual public ritual held on Thanksgiving Eve near the parade route, Mamdani quipped, “It’s the only kind of inflation we support in New York City.”

Will Coss, an executive producer and VP at Macy’s who oversees the retailer’s events, said there will not be a second chance to watch the night-before inflation of the balloons due to the complex logistics of the postponement. He was also asked about the lineup for the event, which could change given that some marching bands (like the one from the University of Albama) are planning to leave town to play at college football games or other events.

The parade is set to include a number of other special guests and celebrities appearing on floats or performing. An “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” will feature performers from new and long-running Broadway productions in a special 10-minute medley.

Coss said it is “an evolving conversation” about potential replacements or planned participants possibly bowing out due to conflicts or travel plans. “We’ve been in communication with all of our participants, from our bands, to our performance groups, to our performing talent. We are optimistic that we’re going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce, and to deliver to New York City.”

The parade remains a major TV draw, with last year’s pulling in 34.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, its biggest combined audience on record. By slotting it in on Saturday morning from 8:30 a.m. to noon ET, NBC should be able to have access to a good-sized audience before college football takes over. Still, the viewership patterns on a more conventional Saturday morning versus those on a weekday holiday with preparations for the Thanksgiving feast providing a supply of captive viewers, will be interesting to watch.

In place of the live event, NBC and Peacock will re-air the 2025 edition of the parade on Thursday morning. Mindful of the unusual dynamic in play this year, the network and streamer will double-run the same ads on both Thursday and Saturday to ensure the scale and impact nets out to a satisfying level for buyers.

It is the first time since it began in 1924 that the parade has ever been postponed. In 1971, balloons were grounded by inclement weather but the parade was still held. World War II forced the cancellation of the parade from 1942 to 1944, and the Covid pandemic in 2020 led to organizers converting it into a television-only event around the Herald Square location of Macy’s Department Store.

This year’s parade is especially significant to Macy’s and NBC, with the latter celebrating its centennial in broadcasting. To help mark the milestone, the parade is set to have 100 of its trademark large balloons.

The importance of NBC’s 100th anniversary is likely to have played a role in the rescheduling. Parent company NBCUniversal, announced early this week that this year’s parade set a revenue record. A windswept and soggy edition of the annual TV fixture would surely have presented myriad production challenges. It possibly would also have left advertisers tuning in to see compromised signage and balloons (some of them branded) swirling precariously around the streets.

“We want to ensure that we’re delivering a parade that’s not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn’t come at the expense of anyone’s safety,” Mamdani said.

#3163. CAD images suggest iPhone 18e will have an odd new camera design

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau …

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

#3161. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

#3160. The Latest Apple Watch Is Up to $100 Off for Black Friday

Apple's latest flagship smartwatch, the Apple Watch Series 12, is worth the upgrade. With this model, Apple has upgraded the processor, added a new heart rate sensor, and improved the display durability. It's certainly one of Apple's best smartwatches, but that also means it isn't cheap: All these new features give the new Series 12 a starting price of $399, which only increases if you choose a model with cellular data. However, for Black Friday, you can take up to $100 off the Series 12, bringing the starting price down to $299.

The three biggest hardware upgrades with the Apple Watch Series 12 are the heart rate sensor, the S11 chip, and Ceramic Shield 2. That heart rate sensor now checks your pulse every five seconds, or 20 times a minute. Apple says the Series 12 checks your heart rate variability 24 times more than the Series 11, and your background heart rate 60 times more frequently than the Series 11. The company is even so bold as to say the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate monitor on a wearable.

Powering the new heart rate monitor is the S11 chip, Apple's latest processor for the Apple Watch. The S11 isn't only responsible for these new heart rate features, however. In addition to running the same watchOS 27 features as other compatible Apple Watches, the S11 on the Series 12 can run Audio Intelligence, Apple's new suite of AI-powered audio features. That includes "Live Rewind," which lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation, and "Siri Recaps," which displays summaries of your conversations throughout the day. Finally, the other major advantage with the Series 12 is Ceramic Shield 2. This is a display upgrade that Apple typically reserves for more premium Apple Watch finishes, but this year, the aluminum Series 12 gets it as well. That means the watch should be more durable against scratches and cracks, without you having to upgrade to the more expensive model.

How much you'll save on a Series 12 depends on the size, color, and model. At this time, Amazon is selling certain colors of the 42mm Series 12 for $299, while certain colors of the 46mm option run $449 (also marked down by $100). You can also save on the cellular models as well: The 42mm option is currently $429 (down from $499), while the 46mm model is $449 (down from $549).

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3159. Judge Sides With ABC In First Amendment Lawsuit Against FCC; Puts Halt To Agency’s Early License Renewal Proceeding

A federal judge has largely sided with ABC in its First Amendment lawsuit claiming that an FCC order to review its broadcast licenses was a retaliatory act by the Trump administration designed to chill its content, whether that be news coverage or jokes from Jimmy Kimmel.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan issued a preliminary injunction on Wednesday that prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in its license review, concluding that the network was “likely to succeed in their retaliation claim.

“This is not a close case,” she wrote in concluding that the network had shown that the public interest favors court intervention in agency action. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'Dancing With The Stars' Finale Recap: Who Takes Home The Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy? Cancellations and Renewals 'Dancing With The Stars: The Next Pro' Renewed For Season 2 At ABC & Prepares To Move Filming To LA

“No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” AliKhan wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

She also rejected the FCC’s effort to dismiss the lawsuit on jurisdictional grounds.

“Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face – loss of their broadcast licenses – the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness,” the judge wrote.

Read the judge’s decision in the ABC case against the FCC.

In highlighting the urgency of court action, AliKhan cited moves that the network has already taken out of fear of losing their licenses. They include the choice to place James Talarico’s guest appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live on YouTube, outside of the FCC’s authority, as well as ABC’s decision to livestream Trump’s July primetime speech out of fear concern of administration retaliation.

“These alterations to Plaintiffs’ editorial decision making showcase how the Commission’s early license renewal proceedings have already curtailed Plaintiffs’ protected activity,” the judge wrote. “That an objectively reasonable broadcaster faced with the same existential threat would follow suit is beyond debate.”

The network is the first major media conglomerate to challenge the FCC’s wave of investigations since the start of Donald Trump‘s second term.

ABC filed suit against the FCC in August, claiming that the agency was violating the First Amendment as it ordered the network’s broadcast stations to submit their licenses to an early review.

The network noted that the agency’s action was unprecedented, creating a chill to its speech and that of other broadcasters given the risk to losing licenses for their eight owned stations. The first of the licenses was not set to expire until 2028.

In claiming regulatory retaliation, the network cited Trump’s attacks on Kimmel and its news coverage, as well as warnings from the president’s FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

The judge referenced Trump’s attacks and warnings in her opinion and noted that three of the co-hosts of The View, as well as Kimmel and ABC News reporters have entrires of the White House’s “media offenders” webpage. She said that Trump and Carr’s “call and response” was “no coincidence.”

She also noted the timing of the FCC’s order for ABC stations to submit to the license review, coming a day after Trump posted on Truth Social that Kimmel should be fired for a skit the previous week.

The FCC has argued that the early license renewal was tied to its inability to obtain documents from the network as part of an investigation of its diversity, equity and inclusion practices. But toward the end of a two-hour hearing last month, the judge asked the agency whether there were other, less drastic alternatives it could have chosen rather than the license review. And in her decision, AliKhan wrote that she did not find the agency’s explanation to be credible.

She wrote, “What is more, Chairman Carr has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders. The same week he was tapped to be President Trump’s FCC chair, following months of President Trump’s calling for ‘ABC [to] lose its license’ for how it covered the presidential campaign …. then-Commissioner Carr lauded ‘license revocation’ as a ‘remedy’ to ‘deter this kind of conduct.'”

During the hearing, Beth Wilkinson, representing the network, compared ABC’s situation to the French Revolution, with people forced on a guillotine, wondering if anything will come down. Losing broadcast licenses, she said, is akin to a “death penalty” for stations.

The FCC argued that the network had to wait until the review process played out before challenging it, and that the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, not the district court, is the venue to hear such a case.

But AliKhan concluded that ABC’s First Amendment retaliation claim fell outside the kind of statutory review set up in the Communications Act, directing challenges to the federal appellate court and likely adding months of delay.

The judge wrote, “To be sure, Plaintiffs would face even greater injury if the FCC ultimately denied their renewal applications. But that does not mean that they are not currently being injured by allegedly being singled out for differential treatment—that is, from facing early license renewal proceedings years in advance of the standard expiration dates as a cudgel to stamp out unfavorable content about President Trump.”

Carr has initiated investigations and reviews of all of the major broadcast networks. Among other things, he launched a probe of The View earlier this year and whether it had to comply with the agency’s Equal Time Rule.

The judge’s decision was limited to the license renewal proceeding. She also denied ABC’s request for a broader injunction that would prohibit any FCC actions “to coerce or threaten” ABC with sanctions as a way to influence their content. AliKhan wrote that such an injunction could not be issued to something “merely feared.”

An ABC News spokesperson said, “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.”

A spokesperson for the FCC said in a statement, “While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear. The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the FCC, said in a statement, “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct. That brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control.”

The case had been closely watched by First Amendment advocates and journalism groups.

Bruce Brown, the president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, called the decision “a big win not only for ABC, but for all broadcasters.”

He said, “As the court recognized, this is ‘not a close case.’ But it is also a novel case forced on ABC because of the administration’s punitive actions and therefore all the more important that the federal judiciary stepped in to vindicate First Amendment rights.

#3158. Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents …

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

#3157. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

Black Friday is the one time of year when TV prices pretty much stop making sense, but in a good way. A TV that cost about a month of rent in January is now closer to a nice dinner out, so if you were patient up until this point, it's about to pay off.

I covered Black Friday sales for years, and these days I spend a lot of my time in the lab at Tom's Guide testing the very same TVs that end up in these sales. That combination has made me picky, but has also given me great deal-finding instincts.

If you only have a moment, here are my two favorite Black Friday TV deals I've seen so far. If your budget is tighter, the Hisense 65M7SR gets you a 65-inch screen for $300 off at Best Buy, which is plenty of TV for most people, especially for just $399.99.

Below you can find even more of my top Black Friday TV deal picks, from OLEDs, to Mini-LEDs, and beyond. Check them out, and for deals on everything else, head to our Black Friday deals hub.

I called the S85H a standout mid-budget OLED when I tested it, and at $500 off, it's an even easier recommendation now. You get the deep blacks and rich color OLED is known for, plus a game mode with VRR and low input lag. Just know there's no Dolby Vision and the built-in speakers are weak, so plan on adding a soundbar (which I would do with any TV, honestly).

LG's latest mid-range OLED is only a marginal upgrade over its predecessor (the LG C5), but this huge discount means you don't have to settle for last year's model. That's a good thing, too, because the C6 is one of the best OLEDs released in 2026. It has all the benefits of OLED technology, like perfect black levels, ultra-wide viewing angles, and an amazing gaming mode.

Sony's Bravia 7 II is the more affordable of its True RGB TVs, and in our testing it delivered deep blacks and well-controlled highlights. This 55-inch model is $900 off right now, which is a steal. Pick one up at Best Buy while the deal lasts.

If you want a decently sized screen without spending much, this LG is a solid place to start. It's a QNED set, which is LG's quantum dot LCD tech, paired with a Mini-LED backlight that should deliver deeper blacks than a standard LED TV. It isn't OLED, but with $110 off at Best Buy, it's a good deal for the price.

This Samsung 65-inch OLED TV is sitting at a crazy discount — just $899.99. That's a great price for any 65-inch OLED TV, let alone one that usually costs over $2,000. While we haven't reviewed the S84H model yet, Samsung consistently makes some of the best OLED TVs on the market.

Finding a name-brand 75-inch TV at this price point is very rare, but Walmart has it covered. The retailer currently has the 75-inch LG UA75 series 4K TV on sale for just $498, down from $528. #3155. If You Loved 'The Good Daughter,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There are plenty of reasons Peacock’s The Good Daughter is so damn watchable. The performances, for one—Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are terrific as estranged sisters Sam and Charlotte Quinn. But it’s also a great story, tracing the corrosive effect of a years-ago trauma on the women and their lawyer father (Brendan Gleeson) amid the slow revelation of many extremely dark secrets. If you want more of that flavor of trauma-driven drama with a tight focus on family bonds, there’s one movie you should watch: 2015's Dark Places.

You want buried secrets? Dark Places has seriously buried secrets. Adapted from the Gillian Flynn novel, the film follows Libby Day (Charlize Theron), who survived the mass murder of her family in 1985. The crime is blamed on her brother Ben, a moody loner whose conviction was based in large part on Libby’s own testimony. For a long time, Libby is financially sustained by donations from people who sympathize with her plight, but three decades after the murders, the money has dried up, and Libby is desperate—so desperate, she agrees to help out a “true crime” club that believes her brother is innocent and is working toward his release.

Like The Good Daughter, Dark Places is anchored by a sibling relationship reshaped by the impact of horrifying violence. Libby and Ben’s experience mirrors Sam and Charlie’s in many ways, including in the way both Libby and Ben carry secrets for years after the terrible events that took family from them. The stories are also both compelling mysteries, slowly revealing the shocking truths behind one horrific night, and ultimately allowing the characters to better understand one another.

Dark Places also explores the insular, suffocating nature of small-town life, and how rumor and gossip become a poisonous presence in people’s lives. Libby, Ben, Sam, and Charlie all have to deal with others' assumptions and revelations that they've been betrayed by those closest to them, leading to powerful resolutions. If you loved The Good Daughter, you’ll love this movie. Stream Dark Places on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more stories about family dynamics around secrets, violence, and explosive emotional confrontations? Here are a few more movies fans of The Good Daughter are bound to enjoy.

There’s no violent crime at the heart of this slow-burn drama—just an explosive chaos agent named Kym, played by Anne Hathaway. If your favorite aspect of The Good Daughter was the relationship between sisters Sam and Charlie, then this movie is perfect. Released from rehab to attend her sister’s wedding, Kym is self-hating, angry, and haunted by a terrible event from her childhood. Her sister, Rachel (Rosemary DeWitt), is welcoming, but has never truly forgiven Kym, and the simmering tension between the sisters and the rest of the family drives a drama that you won’t be able to look away from. Stream Rachel Getting Married on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If you really vibed on the Southern setting, the slow-burn mystery, and the exploration of flawed justice in the modern age depicted in The Good Daughter, check out Where the Crawdads Sing. It’s a slower, dreamier rumination on rural life, violence and its cost, and small-town justice, but it hits the same sweet spot in its story about a woman named Kya (Daisy Edgar-Jones) who was raised in an isolated house in the swamps of North Carolina. Accused in 1969 of a murder, Kya’s story stretches back to her childhood, when she’s slowly abandoned by her entire family, leaving her at age seven to survive on her own. Ostracized as the “swamp girl” by the town, Kya fights to live her life and be loved while facing the unwanted—and violently persistent—attention of the murder victim. It’s about broken families, deeply buried secrets, and what we do to survive. Stream Where the Crawdads Sing on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

The Good Daughter is about life in a small, Southern town, family trauma, and the legal system—which makes A Time to Kill the perfect movie to watch when you finish the show. When a Black man’s daughter is sexually assaulted in Mississippi and her attackers—local members of the Ku Klux Klan—look likely to go free, he violently and publicly murders them. Local lawyer Jake Brigance (Matthew McConaughey) takes on the case, assisted by law student Ellen Roark (Sandra Bullock). They face violent opposition, withering racism, and an unfair legal system that echoes the environment in The Good Daughter in ways fans will appreciate. Stream A Time to Kill on YoutTube or rent it on Prime Video.

The Dry might be as close as you can get to The Good Daughter in terms of tone and story. Although set in Australia instead of the American South, The Dry is a story driven by past crimes and buried secrets in a rural setting just like the show. Twenty years ago, Federal agent Aaron Falk (Eric Bana) fled his hometown when he was suspected of the murder of his girlfriend. When his childhood friend, Luke, appears to have murdered his wife and young son before killing himself, he returns to investigate. The slow revelation of two mysteries—one in the past and one simmering in the drought-stricken present—makes this an ideal companion film to the show. Stream The Dry on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

Set in Boston instead of the South, and focused on male friendships instead of a sisters’ bond, Mystic River nevertheless nails the same atmosphere of dread as The Good Daughter. In 1975, boyhood friends Jimmy, Dave, and Sean are traumatized when Dave is abducted and assaulted by two men. In 1990, the three men remain connected in their Boston neighborhood—Jimmy (Sean Penn) is an ex-convict still connected to local crime, Sean (Kevin Bacon) is a State Police detective, and Dave (Tim Robbins) is a blue-collar worker still haunted by his experience. When Jimmy’s daughter is found murdered and Dave seems implicated, Sean and Jimmy launch investigations from either side of the law, with Dave’s fate hanging in the balance. The ending is powerfully brutal, but this story of secrets and suspicion will resonate with fans of the show. Rent Mystic River on Prime Video.

#3153. iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3151. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

#3149. Ms. Rachel Explains How Mr. Rogers’ “Radical” Programming Inspired Her: “A Huge Responsibility”

As Ms. Rachel continues her mission-driven work, she’s crediting the “radical” influence of Mr. Rogers and her pals on Sesame Street.

The famed YouTube children’s educator and activist (whose real name is Rachel Accurso) recently explained that the “intentional and caring” programming on Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood when she was a kid has inspired her work on the hit Ms. Rachel series.

“When you see Mr. Rogers sharing the pool [with Officer Clemmons], when you when you see on Sesame Street, Black and white children playing together, you’re not like, ‘Wow, that was radical.’ But it was so radical,” she told Hasan Minhaj. “And it’s amazing that I get to be part of a field that is radical, that was pushing those those boundaries.”

Ms. Rachel continued, “I feel honored to be in children’s media and I don’t know if that deep care for children translates to being progressive and being like, ‘Kids should have SNAP benefits. We want kids to eat. We shouldn’t be killing over 20,000 kids in Gaza. They shouldn’t be losing their limbs. And I’m going to show Rahaf on the show and show that she’s just like any other 3-year-old.’ And I think it’s kind of by design that people want to make us think it’s so long ago, but it’s not so long ago. Ruby Bridges is alive and on Instagram.” Watch on Deadline

Noting that Mr. Rogers “knew that children’s media is a huge responsibility and he took that responsibility really seriously” on his PBS series from 1968 to 2001, and even “called out everyone once” at the Emmy Awards, Ms. Rachel admires that he “wasn’t afraid” to tackle serious topics on his show.

“He just was so caring and he really had that pause and he just spoke to children about things that were really serious and he wasn’t afraid to tackle death or assassination or war,” she said.

When people question, “What would Mr. Rogers be now?” Ms. Rachel points out that he dedicated multiple episodes in 1983 to call out the government for spending tax dollars on bombs during anxieties around the Cold War.

“He came out and said it in the show,” she said. “And so, sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, he was subtle. He didn’t come out and say things.’ But he really addressed things in the show more than I do because my show is for younger [kids]. I do have Rahaf on the show. You know, I say things by just having people there. But he really tackled things.”

Ms. Rachel’s comments come as she visited children in immigration court earlier this week, having previously been an outspoken advocate for children in ICE detention centers and Palestinian children in Gaza.

#3147. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

What does the "best mattress deals" mean?

Before I delve into each of the best Black Friday mattress deals, I want to start by clarifying what I mean by the "best mattress deals".

I consider the best mattress deals to A) feature a mattress that was awarded three stars or above by our expert team or online customers and B) meet at least one of the following criteria:

1. It isn't the usual discount — it's better. For example, a mattress that is usually 20% in the regular monthly mattress sales suddenly dropping to 30% off during the Black Friday period.

At Tom's Guide we use a diverse panel of sleep experts to test the most popular mattresses you can find online. We combine repeatable, scientific lab measurements with extended at-home sleep trials. Their review process is also editorially independent and free from brand influence.

Rather than relying solely on first impressions, we use standardized, objective lab tests to generate reliable, unbiased data. For instance, we use thermal imaging camera tests to see how well a mattress regulates temperature, and use accelerometers to test how well a mattress isolates motion.

Lab numbers do not tell the whole story, so a lead reviewer sleeps on each mattress at home for at least three weeks — the typical time it takes for a person's body to adjust to a new bed. #3145. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3144. iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

The iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

#3143. I Tried Coros' New 'Expedition-Focused' Smartwatch, and I'm Impressed

Coros has unveiled the Vertix 4, an “expedition-focused” update to the Vertix 2 and 2S. Coros says it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

This watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

That price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is currently on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that launched earlier this year.

Built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

Previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

Coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:

Music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

On paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.

#3142. Microdrama Revenues Hit $20B, But Profits Outside China Still Weak – MPA Report

The global microdrama business is booming, but outside of China, where ByteDance rules the roost, profits haven’t yet caught with revenues.

That’s according to a Media Partners Asia (MPA) report, which reveals revenues on a global basis are estimated to rise 24% year-on-year to hit $20B in 2026, and that will hit $32B by 2031, a growth rate of 9.8% per year, but profitability is still thin.

The MPA’s second annual Micro-Drama Economy report notes that outside of China, where microdramas first emerged, every 56 cents in a dollar are spent on marketing and another 18 cents goes to app stores and payment providers, which is significantly reducing earnings. Related Stories News Dogwoof Moves Into Microdrama Game With Tattle TV Deal News Women In Vertical Media: Execs From Shorties Studios, aTwist & Eris Join Inaugural Advisory Circle

Excluding China, the microdrama biz is worth $4.87B, with the U.S. the largest at $1.71B, but has fallen 2% year-over-year and will be overtaken by Asia Pacific (excluding China) by 2029. The overall revenue figure will grow to $11B in 2031. Watch on Deadline

The MPA noted the two biggest microdrama groups take revenues of more than $1B a year, but within that DramaBox recorded a net margin of 3.2% in 2025 and ReelShort lost $12M, though it made an $8M profit the first quarter of this year.

DramaBox and GoodShort, which announced a merger at the end of October, along with ReelShort, Kunlun and NetShort collectively account for 65% of revenues outside of China, where the real action is right now. All four apps are Chinese-owned or backed. India is providing the fastest growth, with revenues tripling this year, as local platforms Kuku TV and Story TV boomed and JioStar debuted in the space in April with JioHotstar service Tadka. India is also the largest Asian market outside China with $322M.

MPA’s assessment is that the microdrama business outside of China is not yet settled on a model, but TikTok is predicted to be a dominant force, as it is “positioned on every side” – selling apps’ advertising, carrying their series and, through its free app PineDrama, competing with them.

TikTok’s parent, ByteDance is applying the model that shaped the Chinese market – using free, advertising-funded apps to gain audiences first and monetizing later – and MPA predicts it will gain “significant scale in both the U.S.” and Southeast Asia by 2031. Of course, ByteDance was forced to sell a majority of its shares in TikTok in the U.S., but does retain a minority stake.

YouTube and Meta are not expected to make a major impression on the microdrama space, while locally the likes of Vigloo in Korea and Fuji TV’s Fod Short in Japan are competing with Chinese-backed apps.

China accounts for 76% of total microdrama revenues ($15.2B), following 90% growth in 2025. This will slow to 6.7% in 2031 as viewing plateaus. The MPA doesn’t estimate profits in China as none of the leading players such as top trio ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou single microdrama out in their financing reporting.

Advertising on free services took over paid viewing last year, and this year accounts for 69% of revenues, That will grow to 79% in 2031. ByteDance, which operates Hongguo and Douyin, earning 59% of China’s revenues. ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou collectively account for 82% of the market.

MPA calculates revenue as what viewers, advertisers and brands pay before app-store and payment fees; and outside China it covers dedicated apps and their web stores, not general social feeds. In China, MPA’s estimates exclude producers’ spending on AI models and platform investment, which are both included in the National Radio and Television Administration’s RMB100B estimate for 2025.

“Demand for micro drama is established in every major market, but outside China this is still an emerging business, and it has yet to show that it can earn a durable profit,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and Executive Director of MPA.

“The leading apps spend more than half of their revenue to acquire viewers, and most of those viewers do not pay. Consolidation has begun, and China has already moved to free, advertising-funded viewing. The companies that endure will be those that retain their viewers, bill them directly and invest in titles worth returning to.”

The MPA report raised a further notable asides: new title listings on apps outside China rose from about 100,000 in 2025 to 440,000 in 2026, and 75% were made with AI. This counts series that are made in different languages more than once. MPA’s research shows an AI-made title costs “about a tenth of a series filmed in Los Angeles,” it added.

“AI has made a title cheap enough to test almost any idea, and catalogues have filled accordingly,” said Myat Pan Phyu (May), Lead Analyst, Micro Drama and Vertical Video for MPA. “Viewing has moved far less: live action still dominates the leading titles on most of the platforms we track.

“What decides a platform’s economics is how many of its titles earn back the marketing spent on them. That favours companies with established IP, stars and audiences of their own, which is why local broadcasters, studios and telecom operators matter to the next phase.”
